scenarios.title: Screen from the goalie’s sightline
scenarios.objective: Choose a net-front position that affects the goalie’s view while leaving a passing lane
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. D2 has the puck at the right point. YOU is above the crease, W is low far side, and Gold 1 fronts the shooting lane.
cues: D2 has the puck at the right point.
Gold 1 stands between D2 and the goalie; YOU is above the crease.

questions.prompt: Who is between D2 and the goalie’s net?

options.text: Gold 1
W
D2

questions.explanation: Gold 1 occupies the shooting line, so YOU’s position can change the view without guaranteeing a shot outcome.

questions.prompt: Which two details matter for a useful screen?

options.text: YOU remains between goalie and puck line
YOU leaves D2 a visible lane
YOU stands directly on W

questions.explanation: The screen works through sightline and carrier access; standing on W crowds the net and closes support.

questions.prompt: Arrange one screen read.

options.text: Find D2’s puck line
Set a net-front position outside W’s route
Move if Gold 1 seals the lane

questions.explanation: The puck line shows where screening matters; separation keeps two options; a seal requires a new angle.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly across the crease line to screen without standing on W.
questions.explanation: The crease-side spot changes the goalie’s sightline and leaves W’s low lane visible; if Gold 2 takes it, slide out and reoffer.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 turns to box you out, what could D2 read?

options.text: Whether the changed body position opens W or another lane
That the screen makes the goalie unable to see
That the screen succeeds as soon as YOU stand in front

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s position changes the screen and passing lanes, so D2 updates the option; if none opens, reset.

questions.prompt: How can you screen without turning the play into a collision?
questions.explanation: Stay in the sightline while giving W and D2 separate routes, then move when Gold 1 closes your space; if the lane disappears, re-support.

scenarios.title: Move the puck around the blocked point lane
scenarios.objective: Recognize a blocker and create a different lane before selecting a shot or pass
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. D2 owns the puck at the right point. YOU is between D2 and Gold’s goalie, W is low left, and Gold 1’s stick occupies the direct lane.
cues: Gold 1’s stick is in the straight lane from D2 toward the net.
YOU is in front of the goalie; W is low left.

questions.prompt: What blocks D2’s straight lane?

options.text: Gold 1’s stick and body
W behind the net
The centre red line

questions.explanation: Gold 1 occupies the direct lane, so a lateral move or pass may change it; the other items are outside the stated line.

questions.prompt: Which two alternatives deserve a look?

options.text: Move the puck sideways to change the lane
Use W if the low lane is visible
Shoot through Gold 1 without checking

questions.explanation: Changing the angle or connecting low can move the problem; forcing a blocked lane ignores the defender.

questions.prompt: Order one response to a blocked point lane.

options.text: Locate Gold 1’s stick
Move or pass to change the sightline
Recheck the net-front lane

questions.explanation: The stick identifies the constraint; moving creates new geometry; the final scan tells D2 whether a shot or pass is sensible.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an offset screen position that leaves D2’s lateral lane visible.
questions.explanation: The offset position can occupy a new sightline while leaving D2 a route around Gold 1; if the defender follows, reassess.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows YOU’s lateral move, what changes first?

options.text: The defender’s body may open or close W’s low lane
That D2 must shoot before Gold 1 can recover
That changing your angle guarantees a clear shot

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s movement changes low and point lanes, so D2 scans the new spacing; if both stay closed, reset.

questions.prompt: Why does moving sideways fail if the defender moves with you?
questions.explanation: A lateral move helps only when it changes the defender’s line or opens a teammate, so D2 watches the response; if tracked, use the new support picture.

questions.prompt: Who owns the puck after the short pass?

options.text: F2
YOU
Gold 1

questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to F2 below the dot, so YOU must find a new support angle; if F2 loses it, the offensive read ends.

questions.prompt: Which two details should shape YOU’s reoffer?

options.text: F2’s new puck location
Gold 1’s turn toward F2
The old wall spot staying unchanged

questions.explanation: F2’s location and Gold 1’s response determine the return lane; repeating the old spot can leave the pass behind pressure.

questions.prompt: Arrange one give-and-go reoffer.

options.text: Read F2’s control
Move to a new passing angle
Offer only if the lane stays visible

questions.explanation: Control tells you whether F2 can use support; the new angle changes the lane; a visible lane keeps the reoffer useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU inside and slightly lower than F2 to create a fresh return angle.
questions.explanation: This point shifts YOU inward toward centre ice and slightly below F2, creating a different return angle from Gold 1; if Gold 1 closes it, move high and reoffer.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 steps into the new return lane, what is a sensible next read?

options.text: Whether W or D2 is now clearer support
Whether to pass into Gold 1’s stick
Whether support is no longer needed

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is the visible defender who can remove the new return, so scan W and D2; if neither is available, F2 can protect and wait.

questions.prompt: How do you know your second movement improved the play?
questions.explanation: It should give F2 a visible option away from Gold 1 without crowding W or D2; if it only follows the puck and closes another lane, reset.

questions.prompt: From which side is Gold 1 closing?

options.text: From inside the wall lane
From behind Navy’s net
From the far blue line

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s inside approach is the pressure cue, so YOU can protect toward the wall and look for F2; a different approach would change the turn.

questions.prompt: Which two checks help before turning with the puck?

options.text: Gold 1’s stick side
F2’s support lane
The score from another game

questions.explanation: The pressure side tells you where to place your body and F2 tells you whether a release exists; unrelated score information cannot solve this puck problem.

questions.prompt: Order one protective turn.

options.text: Feel and see Gold 1’s pressure
Place your body between pressure and puck
Use F2 only if the lane is clear

questions.explanation: The pressure read chooses the protective side; body position buys time; F2 becomes useful only when the pass lane is visible.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to the wall while keeping F2 visible.
questions.explanation: The wall-side position shields the puck from Gold 1 and preserves a glance toward F2; if Gold 1 pins the wall, use the high reset.

questions.prompt: If F2 becomes clearly available below you, what might help?

options.text: A short protected pass into F2’s visible lane
A blind pass through Gold 1
Turning away from both puck and support

questions.explanation: F2’s clear lane converts protection into possession; if F2 is covered again, continue protecting or use D2.

questions.prompt: What makes a protective turn useful in this scene?
questions.explanation: The turn moves the puck away from Gold 1 while keeping a reachable support lane, giving YOU time to choose; if no support opens, protection is safer than surrendering the puck.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is inside?

options.text: Gold 1
Gold 2
D1

questions.explanation: Gold 1 carries through the middle, so the inside lane is first; if the carrier moves wide, the picture changes.

questions.prompt: Which two checks matter before closing?

options.text: Gold 1’s lane
D1’s recovery position
Whether D1 will automatically stop the inside pass

questions.explanation: The carrier’s lane and D1’s support determine how you close without giving up middle; noise does not describe the rink.

questions.prompt: Arrange one inside-first gap read.

options.text: See the carrier’s inside route
Keep the carrier outside your body line
Recheck Gold 2 and D1

questions.explanation: The route sets priority; steering outside protects the net-side lane; the second scan updates pass and recovery options.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an inside position between Gold 1 and the Navy net.
questions.explanation: The inside position protects the net while leaving a route to angle Gold 1 wide; if Gold 2 cuts inside, include D1’s help.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 cuts toward the middle, what should YOU reconsider first?

options.text: Whether D1 can take Gold 2 while YOU contains Gold 1
Chasing the puck and losing both lanes
Opening the middle

questions.explanation: Gold 2’s cut creates a coverage decision, so communicate and keep the carrier from the net; if D1 cannot help, stay inside the most dangerous lane.

questions.prompt: Why is the drawn distance alone insufficient for an exact gap?
questions.explanation: The useful gap depends on carrier speed, support and passing lane, which can change after the freeze; if those cues change, closing distance changes too.

findings.issue: Every new-scene briefing uses '+x' and '-x' axis notation in player-facing text. U13 players should receive named-net language.
findings.evidence: All 25 exp26b-u13 briefings begin with 'Navy attacks the +x end and Gold attacks the -x end.'
findings.recommendedChange: Replace that sentence in each new briefing with 'Navy attacks Gold's net and defends Navy's net.' Preserve the actual net and actor geometry while removing coordinate notation from the player-facing scene.

findings.issue: The listed distractors are unrelated trivia, impossible guarantees, or automatic-certainty claims rather than credible U13 hockey decisions.
findings.evidence: Examples include 'The original faceoff result', 'Whether the bench door is open', 'The score from a previous game', 'A guaranteed open net', 'That the shot must go in', 'The goalie’s save is guaranteed', 'Changed teams', and 'The neutral-zone bench'.
findings.recommendedChange: Replace each affected distractor with a plausible nearby choice involving pressure route, support lane, puck protection, coverage handoff, or a conditional branch in that scene. Avoid guaranteed outcomes, irrelevant bench/game trivia, and choices that no player could reasonably select in the shown play.
